newsitem.title: UK: B.A.T confident on U.S. nicotine documents.
newsitem.headline: B.A.T confident on U.S. nicotine documents.

text.p: British tobacco and insurance group B.A.T Industries Plc on Thursday said it was confident that U.S. investigators would not find a "smoking gun" that would show it believed nicotine in cigarettes was addictive.
"We have gone through a very detailed discovery process. Millions of millions of documents have been made available to the plaintiffs attorneys in the U.S.," said B.A.T spokesman Ralph Edmondson.
"I don't believe there is anything else to emerge."

The B.A.T statement follows news late Wednesday that a U.S. judge had restated an investors' lawsuit against Philip Morris Inc that claims the company hid negative information about smoking from investors. U.S. District Judge Michael Mukasey said he restored the suit, originally dismissed in 1995, because of the recent emergence of documents that specifically identified Philip Morris discussing studies about the addictiveness of nicotine.

But B.A.T, which is currently spending $100 million per year defending a plethora of lawsuits in the U.S., noted it had turned over to U.S. authorities around 12 million documents and that investigators had failed to turn up any proof that the company new cigarettes were addictive.

"If there was anything that was relevant, I'm sure plaintiffs attorneys would have brought it to the public's attention by now," Edmondson said. "Our position has not changed. We believe we will prevail in the various lawsuits we are defending in the U.S."

B.A.T shares, which were down 9-1/2p to 507 by 0900 GMT, have dropped 11 percent since mid-March when U.S. rival Liggett Group became the first tobacco company to admit smoking was additive and could cause cancer.
